summary: This document defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing a client that uses the iSCSI protocol. It obsoletes RFC 4544.

eli5.summary: This is a list of dials and gauges that let administrators check and manage an iSCSI client from a management program.

questions: which snmp notifications does iscsi define
how do iscsi portals work in the mib
subtitle: The SNMP object model for managing iSCSI portals, nodes, sessions and connections.

tldr.problem: Administrators need a standard way to configure, monitor and troubleshoot devices that use iSCSI, and the earlier MIB no longer matched the updated iSCSI specification.
tldr.mechanism: It defines a MIB module, rooted at { mib-2 142 }, that organizes iSCSI as instances, portals, nodes, targets, initiators, sessions and connections, with separate attribute and statistics tables and three notifications.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4544 and brings the module in line with RFC 7143, adding new session attributes and counters.

facts.label: Notification rate limit
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed 3 in any 10-second period

today: RFC 7147 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. It obsoletes RFC 4544, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the iSCSI MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 7147 defines a MIB module (Management Information Base) for managing devices that implement the iSCSI protocol. MIB objects are normally accessed through SNMP, and this module is written in SMIv2.

The module supplies configuration, fault and statistics information, structured around familiar iSCSI things: targets, initiators, sessions and connections. It can also be used to configure access to targets by creating portals and authorization list entries.

It is deliberately an iSCSI-only module. It has no SCSI-layer attributes, which belong to the SCSI MIB. It also does not count everything: only counters useful for finding performance, security and fault problems from a management station.
sections.eli5: It is a standard control panel layout, so any management program can read the same gauges on any iSCSI device.

sections.title: Relationship to Other MIB Modules
sections.content:
The iSCSI MIB is normally layered between the SCSI MIB module and the TCP MIB module, and it uses the IP Storage (IPS) Identity Authentication MIB module.

  • SCSI MIB: each iSCSI node is related to one SCSI device. The iscsiNodeTransportType attribute points to the SCSI transport object, which points back, so a management station can navigate both ways.
  • TCP MIB: each iSCSI connection relates to one TCP connection through its 5-tuple of protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port.
  • AUTH MIB: a target's list of authorized initiators, and an initiator's list of targets to contact, point to identities in the IPS-AUTH module.

Every non-scalar object is indexed first by an iSCSI instance, which can be a physical or virtual partition of a device. Instances do not replace SNMP contexts, but they make it simple to assign a partition to one or more contexts.
sections.eli5: This control panel plugs into other panels: one for the disk, one for the network connection and one for the guest list.

sections.title: The Object Model and Tables
sections.content:
The top-level object is the iSCSI instance, which contains everything else. Inside it are portals, which are IP addresses used by the instance, and nodes. A node can be an initiator, a target or both, and a session is an active link between an initiator and a target. A session may be Inbound or Outbound, and each session contains its active TCP connections.

Each object has an attributes table and zero or more statistics tables that augment it. Keeping them separate lets attributes and statistics grow independently. Examples are login and logout statistics for targets and initiators, a session statistics table that counts requests, responses and bytes, and a session connection error table that counts digest and connection errors.

The instance attributes table is the primary table. Most implementations will have just one row, but it exists to allow multiple virtual instances. Session types are normal sessions or discovery sessions using SendTargets. No statistics are kept for connections.
sections.eli5: Think of a school with classrooms, teachers and students. The MIB lists each one and keeps a separate scoreboard for them.

sections.title: Portals, Nodes and Access Control
sections.content:
A portal is an IP address (v4 or v6) plus a transport protocol, currently only TCP. A portal row has a roles attribute, iscsiPortalRoles. Setting the targetTypePortal bit makes the implementation start listening for iSCSI connections. Setting initiatorTypePortal does not necessarily cause connections; the implementation decides whether and when to use it. Both bits can be set.

Management stations can create and delete portal rows. The matching initiator and target portal rows are then created and destroyed automatically. Deleting a portal terminates its connections, either at once or by a clean shutdown as specified in RFC 7143. Objects in an active row cannot be modified, so changing a portal's IP address means deleting and creating rows.

Target portals carry a listen port and a portal group aggregation tag. Target portals that share a tag can hold connections of the same session. Each target has a list of initiator identities allowed to access it, and each initiator has a list of targets it should connect to. Both lists point to identities in the IPS-AUTH module.
sections.eli5: A portal is a door. The MIB lets you add or remove doors and keep a list of who is allowed to come through.

sections.title: Addresses and Descriptors
sections.content:
IP addresses are represented by a pair of attributes, an InetAddressType and an InetAddress, so that IPv4 and IPv6 are both supported. Port numbers are stored as plain port numbers beside a protocol attribute, so the module can be used with transports other than TCP in future.

Some attributes, such as the digest methods, would normally be enumerations. To let vendors add their own schemes, they are instead object identifiers pointing at object identities in the iscsiDescriptors subtree. An implementation that adds its own method should define a matching object identity in its enterprise MIB and return that OID when it is in use.

The module also defines textual conventions, including IscsiName for iSCSI names, whose size is 0 or 16 to 223 octets, where a zero-length string means no name.
sections.eli5: Instead of a fixed list of choices, each choice has a unique ID badge, so makers of other devices can create new choices without breaking the list.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
Three notifications are defined. iscsiTgtLoginFailure is sent when a target fails a login, iscsiIntrLoginFailure when an initiator does, and iscsiInstSessionFailure when an active session is failed by either side because of a connection or digest failure.

The login notifications are meant for critical failures, those that may expose security-related problems needing immediate action, such as authentication, authorization or negotiation failures. Attributes on the initiator, target and instance objects carry the information to send, such as the name and address of the other end.

An SNMP agent SHOULD NOT send more than three iSCSI notifications in any 10-second period. The RFC explains the choice: one notification every three seconds was deemed often enough, while a short burst of different notifications should not be suppressed.
sections.eli5: These are alarm bells. To stop the alarm from ringing nonstop, it is only allowed to ring a few times in a short while.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access can be sensitive. The portal tables can add or remove IP addresses used by iSCSI, and the target authorization table can add or remove access for initiators. Setting them without proper protection can harm network operations.

Some readable objects are also sensitive. The node, target and target authorization tables can reveal what is needed to connect to the targets. The RFC points out that initiators and targets must still authenticate each other, as discussed in RFC 7143.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and those claiming SNMPv3 compliance MUST fully support authentication and privacy with the User-based Security Model using the AES cipher. They MAY also support the Transport Security Model with a secure transport such as SSH or TLS/DTLS.
sections.eli5: The control panel can change who gets in, so only trusted people should be allowed to touch it, and its messages should be kept private.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4544
sections.content:
RFC 7147 obsoletes RFC 4544. RFC 7143 updated several RFCs, including RFC 3720, and this document updates the MIB to match. It uses the iSCSIProtocolLevel defined in RFC 7144.

  • Added iscsiInstXNodeArchitecture to the instance attributes.
  • Added iscsiSsnTaskReporting (type BITS) and iscsiSsnProtocolLevel to the session attributes.
  • Deprecated the marker objects.
  • Added NOP counters at session scope for heartbeat tracking.
  • Added a port number to the login failure notifications and added a description string to the portal.
  • Added counters for Target Unmapped session failures and for Logout Commands with reason codes 1 and 2.
  • Fixed errata to RFC 4544 and updated the conformance statements.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the control panel with a few new gauges, and a few old, unused ones marked as going away.

root.label: iscsiInstance
root.note: A distinct iSCSI entity within the managed system

children.label: iscsiPortal
children.note: An IP address used by this instance

children.label: iscsiInitiator
children.note: Has iscsiIntrAuth, the targets to contact

children.label: iscsiSession
children.note: Contains iscsiConnection, an active TCP connection
